destinations.name: Buenos Aires
destinations.justification: National tourism confirms continuing international operations during the October 25–November 11, 2026 runway works. City tourism identifies Ministro Pistarini/EZE as the long-haul arrival airport and documents taxis, private transfers and Tienda Leon city buses. AEP is a valid closer alternative for domestic and neighbouring-country arrivals; EZE remains a defensible broad international default. Runway works may cause technical stops on some long-haul departures; confirm the travel-date itinerary.
reviewNotes: A practical default, not a guarantee of nonstop service, fares or availability from every origin/date. Trip.com live search was not exercised; this is a physical-airport destination-code mapping.

arrival.title: International Arrival
arrival.note: Most international flights arrive at  (EZE), located approximately 45–60 minutes from the city centre depending on traffic.

arrival.title: Domestic & Regional Flights
arrival.note: Some regional or domestic connections arrive at  (AEP), much closer to central neighbourhoods.

gettingAround: Walking is the primary way to understand Buenos Aires—wide sidewalks, long blocks, and visible street life define orientation.
Taxis and ride-hailing apps are widely used, affordable, and often preferred over public transport, especially at night or in heat.
The Subte (metro) is efficient for longer crossings but less expressive of neighbourhood texture.
Buses are extensive but complex for short stays; use only if familiar or with local guidance.
Late evenings and nights rely heavily on taxis—public transport frequency drops after midnight.

arrival.note: Most travellers arrive via  (FTE), located about 20 minutes from El Calafate by shuttle or taxi.

gettingAround: El Calafate town is small—walking works for lakeside paths, restaurants, and basic orientation.
Perito Moreno Glacier requires organised transport: shuttle buses, small-group tours, or private transfers are standard.
El Calafate to El Chaltén is a long-distance road journey (≈3 hours) through open steppe—public buses, private transfers, or rental cars are used.
El Chaltén village is compact—most trails begin on foot directly from accommodation.
There is no meaningful public transport within El Chaltén—walking is the default mode.

Taxis are available but often unnecessary due to Nice’s compact layout.

arrival.title: International Arrival → Paris
arrival.note: Paris is served by Charles de Gaulle (CDG) and Orly (ORY) airports, both well connected to the city by train and bus. Rail arrival via Gare du Nord, Gare de Lyon, or Gare Montparnasse is also common from within Europe.

arrival.title: Airport → City Centre
arrival.note: RER B connects Charles de Gaulle directly to central Paris in around 35–45 minutes. Orly is served by Orlyval + RER or direct bus services. Taxis are convenient but slower during peak traffic hours.

gettingAround: Walking is essential—many of Paris’s best moments happen between landmarks, especially along the Seine and within neighbourhood streets.
The métro is fast, dense, and intuitive; it is usually quicker than taxis for cross-city travel.
Buses offer scenic above-ground routes and are useful when you want to see the city while moving.
Taxis and ride-hailing apps are widely available but can be slow in traffic-heavy central areas.
Cycling and e-scooters exist but are less comfortable for first-time visitors in dense districts.

arrival.note: The city centre is compact. From the airport, the tram reaches Santa Maria Novella station in about 20 minutes. From the station, most accommodation is walkable.

gettingAround: Walking is the primary way to experience Florence—distances are short and the city reveals itself best at human pace.
Buses are useful for hills or longer hops (e.g., toward Boboli edges or Piazzale Michelangelo).
Taxis are practical late evening or in heat but unnecessary for most daytime movement.
Cycling is possible but less common inside the historic core due to narrow streets and crowds.
Private vehicles are strongly discouraged within the historic centre.

arrival.title: Arrival → Venice
arrival.note: Venice is reached via Marco Polo Airport (VCE) or by train to Venezia Santa Lucia. The train station opens directly onto the Grand Canal, providing an immediate sense of place.

arrival.title: Airport → Historic Venice
arrival.note: Water buses (Alilaguna) and water taxis connect the airport to the city. Water taxis are faster but expensive; Alilaguna is slower but atmospheric and practical for first-time arrivals.

gettingAround: Walking is the primary way to experience Venice—distances are short, but routes are indirect by design.
Vaporetto water buses are essential for longer canals and lagoon edges; treat rides as part of the experience, not just transport.
There are no cars, bicycles, or taxis within the historic city—movement happens at human or water speed.
Expect detours: bridges, dead ends, and canals are part of Venice’s logic, not obstacles.
Luggage should be kept light—stairs and bridges are unavoidable.

arrival.note: Most common: limited express or rapid train via Otsuki, then Fujikyu Railway to Fujisan or Shimoyoshida Station (about 2–2.5 hours total). Highway buses from Shinjuku are also direct and convenient.

gettingAround: Walking works well within Fujiyoshida town for street-level Mount Fuji views and short neighbourhood routes.
Local buses connect Fujiyoshida with Chureito Pagoda, Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine, and Lake Kawaguchi.
Taxis are useful for early-morning starts or when visibility windows are short—distances are small but time-sensitive.
Cycling is possible in flatter areas, but elevation changes and cold mornings limit comfort.

Taxis are useful for short transfers to ryokan or when weather disrupts transport links.

arrival.title: Tokyo / Osaka → Kyoto
arrival.note: From Tokyo: Shinkansen to Kyoto Station (about 2–2.5 hours). From Osaka: JR Special Rapid (30 minutes) or Hankyu/Keihan lines depending on district.

gettingAround: Walking is central to the Kyoto experience—temple grounds, stone lanes, and neighbourhood streets are best explored on foot.
Buses are essential for reaching temple areas not directly served by trains, especially in Higashiyama and central Kyoto.
Trains work well for longer moves, such as Kyoto Station to Arashiyama or Fushimi areas.
Taxis are useful for short hops between nearby temples or when avoiding heat, but traffic can slow them during peak hours.

arrival.title: Primary Access Routes

gettingAround: Movement in the Sacred Valley is road-based; distances between sites are too large for walking between villages.
Taxis, private drivers, or small group vans are the most practical and common transport options.
Public colectivos exist between major towns (Pisac, Urubamba, Ollantaytambo) but are slower and less flexible for site access.
Once at each site or village, exploration is primarily on foot.
Lower altitude than Cusco noticeably reduces fatigue, but terrace climbs still demand pacing.
